questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=4{x}^{2}y,\,y(0)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=0.5,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **general form** of $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ in terms of the new values ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and the current values $x$ and $y?$
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}^{2}y+4({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}{y}_{\text{new}})\cdot 0.5 \\  & ={x}^{2}y+({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+{x}^{2}y+({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}{y}_{\text{new}},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{{{y}_{\text{new}}-({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}{y}_{\text{new}}-y-{x}^{2}y}_{⏟}}_{g({y}_{\text{new}})}=0.
$$

Therefore, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.5$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}{y}_{\text{new}}-y-{x}^{2}y.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=4{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2})\cdot 1 \\  & =2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+2{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+2{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-2{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-y-2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-2{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-y-2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

 Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-2(2)^{2}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-1-2(1)^{2}(1)^{2} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-8({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-{y}^{3},\,y(0.5)=1
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(1).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(1)≈$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=1,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=1-0.5=0.5.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((2x-{y}^{3})+(2{x}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}))\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5x-0.25{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5x-0.25{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.25{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5x=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.5$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.25{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}-0.5x.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0.5+0.5=1.
$$

Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.25(1)^{3}-1-0.5\cdot 1-0.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=0.75({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.25(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-1.5}{0.75(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+1}
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0.5)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & ≈1.142\,857 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.134\,757 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.134\,728\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈1.13,$ rounded to two decimal places.

Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x+{y}^{2},\,y(0)=0
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(0.4).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(0.4)≈$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0.4,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=0.4-0=0.4.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((x+{y}^{2})+({x}_{\text{new}}+({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}))\cdot 0.4 \\  & =0.2x+0.2{y}^{2}+0.2{x}_{\text{new}}+0.2({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.2x+0.2{y}^{2}+0.2{x}_{\text{new}}+0.2({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.2({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}+y+0.2x+0.2{y}^{2}+0.2{x}_{\text{new}}=0.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $5$ to eliminate the decimals, we obtain

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-5{y}_{\text{new}}+5y+x+{y}^{2}+{x}_{\text{new}}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.4$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-5{y}_{\text{new}}+5y+x+{y}^{2}+{x}_{\text{new}}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+0.4=0.4.
$$

Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-5{y}_{\text{new}}+5\cdot 0+0+{0}^{2}+0.4 \\  & =({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-5{y}_{\text{new}}+0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=0$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=2({y}_{\text{new}})-5.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}-5({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}+0.4}{2({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-5}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=0,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =0 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =0.08 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈0.081\,322 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈0.081\,323\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(0.4)≈0.08,$ rounded to two decimal places.

{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1.
$$

 Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5(1)^{3}-1-1.5\cdot 1-1.5\cdot 0 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5-1-1.5 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=1.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-2}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =1.2 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.179\,747 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.179\,509\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈1.18,$ rounded to two decimal places.

Consider the following initial value problem:

questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((2x+{y}^{3})+(2{x}_{\text{new}}+({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}))\cdot 1 \\  & =x+0.5{y}^{3}+{x}_{\text{new}}+0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+x+0.5{y}^{3}+{x}_{\text{new}}+0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{y}_{\text{new}}+y+x+0.5{y}^{3}+{x}_{\text{new}}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{y}_{\text{new}}+y+x+0.5{y}^{3}+{x}_{\text{new}}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

 Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{y}_{\text{new}}+(-1.5)+1+0.5(-1.5)^{3}+2 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{y}_{\text{new}}-1.5+1-1.6875+2 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{y}_{\text{new}}-0.1875.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=-1.5$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=1.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}-({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-0.1875}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}-1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(1)=-1.5,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =-1.5 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & ≈-1.342\,105 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈-1.310\,301 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈-1.309\,019\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈-1.31,$ rounded to two decimal places.

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 2y^2 - \sqrt{x}, \qquad y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $\Delta x = 1,$ the new value $y_\text{new}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g(y_\text{new}) = 0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g(y_\text{new})$ used in the first step?

- $g(y_\text{new}) = y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^2 - 1 + \dfrac12\sqrt{2}$

- $g(y_\text{new}) = y_\text{new} - \dfrac12 (y_\text{new})^2 - \dfrac32 + \dfrac12\sqrt{2}$

- $g(y_\text{new}) = y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^2 - \dfrac32 + \dfrac12\sqrt{2}$

- $g(y_\text{new}) = y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^2 - \dfrac32 - \dfrac12\sqrt{2}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta y = \dfrac12(y' + y'_\text{new}) \cdot \Delta x,
$$

with $y'_\text{new} = f(x_\text{new},y_\text{new})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $\Delta y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2{y}^{2}-\sqrt{x}+2({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}})\cdot 1 \\  & ={y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x}+({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{x}+({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^2 - y - y^2 + \dfrac12\sqrt{x} + \dfrac12\sqrt{x_\text{new}} = 0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $\Delta x = 1$ is

$$
g(y_\text{new}) = y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^2 - y - y^2 + \dfrac12\sqrt{x} + \dfrac12\sqrt{x_\text{new}}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x = 1 + 1 = 2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-1-{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 2 - xy^2, \qquad y(1)=1
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(2).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta y = \dfrac12(y' + y'_\text{new}) \cdot \Delta x,
$$

with $y'_\text{new} = f(x_\text{new},y_\text{new})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
\Delta x = 2 - 1 = 1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $\Delta y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((2-x{y}^{2})+(2-{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4-x{y}^{2}-{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}) \\  & =2-0.5x{y}^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+2-0.5x{y}^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5x_\text{new}(y_\text{new})^2 + y_\text{new} - y - 2 + 0.5xy^2 = 0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $\Delta x = 1$ is

$$
g(y_\text{new}) = 0.5x_\text{new}(y_\text{new})^2 + y_\text{new} - y - 2 + 0.5xy^2.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x = 1 + 1 = 2.
$$

 Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5\cdot 2\,({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1-2+0.5\cdot 1\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g(y_\text{new}) = 0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
(y_\text{new})_{n+1} = (y_\text{new})_n - \dfrac{g(y_\text{new})}{g'(y_\text{new})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
g'(y_\text{new}) = 2(y_\text{new}) + 1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
(y_\text{new})_{n+1}
= (y_\text{new})_n
- \dfrac{((y_\text{new})_n)^2 + (y_\text{new})_n - 2.5}
       {2(y_\text{new})_n + 1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(1) = 1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & ≈1.166\,667 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.158\,333 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.158\,312\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2) \approx \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1.16},$ rounded to two decimal places.
